title: Subword Tokenization with Byte-Pair Encoding
hook: Whole words make a giant vocabulary; single characters make long sequences. Subwords split the difference — and let models read words they've never seen.
key_points: Splits text into frequent subword chunks instead of whole words or single characters.
Builds the vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most common adjacent pairs.
Rare or unseen words break into known pieces, so nothing is truly out-of-vocabulary.
Keeps the vocabulary small while still covering open vocabularies — used by most LLMs.
content_html: Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch adapted byte-pair encoding to tokenize text into subword units rather than whole words or single characters. The vocabulary is built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pairs, so common words stay intact while rare ones break into familiar pieces. This lets models handle unseen words with a compact vocabulary, and it's how most large language models read text today.
extra_html:
How it works

You start by treating each word as a sequence of characters, then count which adjacent symbol pairs appear most often and merge the top one into a single new token. Repeat this thousands of times and frequent character sequences fuse into subword units — common words may become one token while uncommon ones stay split into reusable pieces. At inference, any word, even one never seen in training, can be encoded as some combination of these learned subwords.

Why it matters

Earlier systems struggled with out-of-vocabulary words, names, and morphologically rich languages because a fixed word list can never cover everything. Subword tokenization removes that hard wall while keeping the vocabulary small enough to be practical. The approach proved so effective that it, and close relatives, became the default way modern language models turn text into tokens.
